entities.name: Ka'b bin Zuhayr
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr, a pre-eminent Arabian poet of the 7th century CE, stands as a pivotal figure in the transition from pre-Islamic (Jahiliyya) poetic traditions to the nascent literary landscape of Islam. Born into the esteemed Banu Fahm tribe, renowned for its poets, Kaʿb inherited a rich oral tradition, initially using his formidable talent to satirize the burgeoning Islamic movement and its prophet, Muhammad. His dramatic conversion to Islam and subsequent composition of the panegyric qasida, 'Bānat Suʿād' (Suʿād Has Departed), marked a watershed moment, not only in his personal trajectory but also in establishing a new paradigm for poetic expression within the Islamic era.

Following a period of exile and a death sentence pronounced by the Prophet Muhammad for his earlier satirical verses, Kaʿb made a perilous journey to Medina around 630 CE to seek forgiveness. He boldly presented himself before Muhammad, reciting 'Bānat Suʿād,' a masterwork of praise that skillfully blends traditional desert imagery with an eloquent apology and affirmation of faith. The poem's climax saw Muhammad bestow his personal cloak (burda) upon Kaʿb, a profound gesture of reconciliation and acceptance that instantly elevated the poet's status and sanctified the qasida itself as a foundational text of Islamic panegyric.

The gift of the Prophet's cloak, known as the 'Burdat al-Nabi,' transformed 'Bānat Suʿād' into a sacred artifact of Islamic literature, inspiring countless subsequent poets to compose their own 'burda' poems in praise of Muhammad. This act established a powerful precedent for the integration of poetry into the Islamic intellectual and spiritual sphere, demonstrating how literary talent could be harnessed to serve religious devotion. Kaʿb's qasida thus became a cornerstone of classical Arabic literature, studied for its linguistic artistry, its historical context, and its profound influence on the development of Islamic poetic forms.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ka'b bin Zuhayr's poem 'Bānat Suʿād' profoundly shaped the genre of Islamic panegyric and became a foundational text for understanding early Muslim-poet interactions, influencing centuries of Arabic literature and establishing the symbolic 'burda' tradition.
